name: Knocker
lore: One of the night shift Knappers' Deep lost to the Fall, still at the face with his pick. The Vale buries its dead with their tools so they have something to be known by; these were never buried, and their tools were in their hands. They knock on the chalk in the night shift's count, seven and then one, and they come to anything with a light the way a miner comes to the lamp at the end of a shift. The chalk has got into them. They are as white as the walls.

name: Barrow-Digger
lore: The diggers go where the Wardens' map says there is something old under the turf, and take the turf off it. Orm's Long Barrow was theirs, and Tallow Barrow, until whatever was in Tallow walled itself back in. They are Larkbourne Boys who found that the dead pay better than carters and do not send for the Wardens. They carry spades sharpened on one edge, and they fight the way they dig: in a hurry, before anybody comes.

name: Wakeless
lore: One of the Ash Winter's dead, carried up Hound Down in the hungry winter and laid in Wake Barrow without a wake, because there were too many and nobody had the strength. The Vale sat three nights with its dead so they would know they were dead. These were never told. They are thin as the winter left them, wound in their shrouds, and they go about the barrow the way the newly dead go about a house: looking for someone to sit with them.

name: Wassailer
lore: One of the Vale folk who went down the cellar stair at Wassail Knap behind the last Wassail King, forty Twelfth Nights ago, or one of the pickers who have followed the singing down since. They are still at the wassail: flushed, ragged, wreathed in dead apple-twigs, a cup in every hand. They do not want to hurt you. They want you to dance, and to drink, and never to go home, and they hold on.

name: Sheaf-Man
lore: A figure of bound straw the height of a man, wound out of the rotted tithe sheaves in the Great Barn's undercroft, with a reaping-hook bound into one arm. The Vale makes a kern-baby of the last sheaf to keep the harvest's life over winter; nobody carried the last one out, and the life went into the rest of the straw. They cut whatever is growing, ripe or not, and stand the sheaves up facing the barn. They burn like the straw they are.
